extracted.intended_audience: general readers, federal agency staff, administrative law students, and practitioners interested in rulemaking processes
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the U.S. federal negotiated rulemaking ("neg reg") process: when agencies choose it, how committees are formed and facilitated, drafting and consensus rules, statutory basis, and empirical assessments of its success and critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision to use negotiated rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually, an agency is not mandated to use negotiated rulemaking; its decision to use negotiated rulemaking is not subject to review by the courts. The decision to use negotiated rulemaking is based on a number of factors, including whether it is likely that a balanced committee can be formed and whether it is reasonable to believe that the committee will reach a consensus recommendation for a proposed rule. The agency's resources are also considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies choose neg reg voluntarily. Consider whether a balanced committee can be formed, the likelihood of consensus, and available agency resources when deciding to initiate neg reg. (Citation needed noted in source for some claims.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of a balanced advisory committee
rubrics_metrics.description: A balanced committee of representatives from the agency and affected interest groups is required for neg reg to be effective; the list of proposed advisory committee members is published and subject to public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed committee members and issues must be published in the Federal Register and are open to public comment; people who feel under-represented on the committee can request membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a convener to assess feasibility and propose participants
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of a convener to determine the feasibility of undertaking a negotiated rulemaking is authorized under the Negotiated Rulemaking Act. A convener may also recommend a list of stakeholder representatives for participation on the neg reg advisory committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may rely on a neutral convener's feasibility assessment and representative recommendations, though sometimes the agency compiles its own list of potential participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication in the Federal Register and follow-on notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency publishes the proposed rule in the Federal Register and then follows the usual rulemaking procedure of soliciting public comments, which are evaluated for inclusion in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication of proposed advisory committee members and issues is also required; this public notice allows stakeholders to request membership and to comment on issues to be negotiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground rules for the negotiating committee
rubrics_metrics.description: Once established under the Federal Advisory Committee Act, the committee prepares a set of ground rules, which include the committee's deadline, mission, responsibilities, commitments, and a decision rule or definition of consensus. A final list of the issues to be negotiated is also created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear deadlines, mission statements, responsibilities, commitments, and an explicit decision rule/definition of consensus before substantive negotiation begins to structure the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitation by a public policy mediator
rubrics_metrics.description: Neg Regs are facilitated by a public policy mediator who provides focus and manages the negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A neutral mediator helps manage discussions, keep parties focused, and can enable face-to-face interaction and cooperation that allows parties to share information and leverage committee members' skill sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of background materials to negotiators
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiators are provided with relevant background materials to inform discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide comprehensive, relevant background documents to participants so negotiations proceed from a shared factual and technical foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting and iterative development of regulatory text
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee discusses each issue striving for agreements in concept, which government staff draft as regulatory text. This draft text is reviewed and revised until a tentative consensus agreement is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government staff should translate conceptual agreements into draft regulatory text and iterate with the committee until tentative consensus is obtained. If early consensus cannot be reached, the drafting team should outline multiple options discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency check before final consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: When tentative agreements are reached on all issues, the agreements are checked for consistency before final consensus is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform cross-issue consistency reviews to ensure mutually compatible provisions prior to declaring final consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical timeline and meeting cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiated rulemaking typically takes six months to a year and involves multi-day meetings approximately once a month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for a multi-month engagement with periodic multi-day meetings (roughly monthly) when scheduling and resourcing a neg reg effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion to adopt committee proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency can publish a proposal adopted by its negotiating committee, but the Negotiated Rulemaking Act does not require it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that committee consensus is advisory; the agency retains discretion whether to publish or adopt committee-proposed rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Negotiated Rulemaking Act (1990, reauthorized 1996) is incorporated into the Administrative Procedure Act at 5 U.S.C. §§ 561-570. Negotiated rulemaking is currently required under the Higher Education Act and the Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the statutory authorization and any statutory mandates for particular subject areas when considering or conducting neg reg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of success and empirical evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for neg reg include decreased litigation and more expeditious rulemaking; empirical studies have produced mixed results (e.g., one study reported 50% of negotiated rules resulted in litigation vs. ~25% overall, and no time savings), while other researchers and practitioners report benefits such as improved perceived rule quality, accuracy, and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple metrics (litigation rates, time-to-promulgation, perceived rule quality, stakeholder satisfaction) and be cautious: empirical evidence on benefits is contested and studies may differ in methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism regarding special-interest influence and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A criticism of negotiated rulemaking is that it subverts the public interest because special interest groups have too much sway; others argue that 'public interest' is too vague to be a useful variable in assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and address concerns about disproportionate influence by particular stakeholders; ensure transparency, representativeness, and opportunities for public input to mitigate perceptions of capture.
